title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at what many consider Dickens's darkest, strangest, and most brilliant novel.
Our Mutual Friend was published in 1864 and 1865, the last novel Dickens completed before his death — and it reads like a writer who has nothing left to prove and everything left to say.
Today we're beginning at the beginning — with the novel's great obsessions: money, dust, and the strange possibility of resurrection.
Joining me are three readers who bring very different things to the table, and I'm delighted to introduce them.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Dickens as a performer, hearing the rhythms, the comic timing, the grotesques.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong literary traditionalist who believes novels are above all stories about moral character tested by circumstance.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he's interested in what the system produces, and who pays the price.
Gentlemen, let's begin with the novel's strange opening image — a boat drifting on the Thames, and a man dragging bodies from the river for money.
What I love about that opening — and I've read it aloud more times than I can count — is that Dickens gives you the whole novel in miniature within the first three pages.
You have Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie out on the river at night, and Gaffer is towing something behind the boat.
And Dickens, with that marvellous precision of his, describes Gaffer's relationship to his grim harvest in terms that are entirely commercial.
He tells us that Gaffer looked at his work with the air of an expert — 'not without a certain pride.'
'Not without a certain pride.'
It's the pride of a craftsman, a professional — dragging corpses for their pocket contents — and that collision of the mercantile and the macabre is absolutely characteristic of this novel.
Dickens is telling you from the very first page: in this world, everything has a price, and the dead are no exception.
And what strikes me about that opening is how precisely Dickens locates labour in it.
Gaffer Hexam is a working man who extracts value from the river — from the dead deposited there by a city that has used them up and thrown them away.
The Thames in this novel is not a picturesque backdrop — it's an industrial sewer and a burial ground, and the men who work it are at the absolute bottom of the social order.
What's remarkable is that Dickens frames the entire plot — the inheritance of old Harmon's dust fortune — through this same lens of extraction.
Old Harmon made his fortune from dust heaps — from the waste matter of a city — and his heir's supposed death in the river ties these two images of salvage together from the very start.
The novel is asking: who owns the dead, who owns the waste — and who profits?
I don't wish to quarrel with that reading, but I think it risks flattening something that is, at its heart, a moral investigation.
The river opening is undeniably arresting, but what Dickens is staging there is a question about the corruption of the soul — not merely of the economy.
Gaffer Hexam has a code — a crooked one, but a code nonetheless.
He distinguishes himself, with great indignation, from those who rob the dead — he merely takes what the dead no longer need.
That self-justification is the novel's great subject — the stories people tell themselves about money and what they deserve.
And Dickens, being a moralist of the first order, traces those stories with extraordinary patience — from Gaffer on the river, all the way up to the Veneerings in their brand-new dining room.
The Veneerings — now there's a gift.
Dickens introduces them in that second chapter with a sustained comic attack that I find genuinely irresistible.
Everything in the Veneering house is brand new — the carriages, the plate, the guests, the very cutlery seems to have been minted yesterday.
Dickens writes of Mr. and Mrs. Veneering that they were 'bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.'
'Bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.'
The triple repetition of 'bran-new' — the archaic spelling emphasising the rawness, the newness, the lack of any history — it's comic writing of the highest order.
And it tells you everything about what money without tradition looks like in Dickens's world.
And the Veneerings' dinner party is where Dickens shows the machinery of social reproduction operating in real time.
Everyone at that table is performing — performing wealth, performing connection, performing the fiction that they belong.
And the Analytical Chemist — the butler who moves through the dinner with barely concealed contempt — is Dickens's way of placing a sceptical observer inside the spectacle.
He offers the wine as if he were suggesting that the guests might consider poison — and that dark undercurrent is entirely deliberate.
The wealth on display at the Veneering table is built on the same principles as Gaffer's river work — take what you can, ask no questions, and call it respectable.
There is something to that, though I would put it differently.
What Dickens understood — and here I think he is closer to Burke than to Marx — is that a society without inherited forms, without the tested weight of tradition, becomes a society of masks.
The Veneerings are terrifying not because they are capitalists, but because they have no selves — the veneer goes all the way down.
And against that, Dickens sets figures like Betty Higden or Lizzie Hexam — people of genuine moral substance, precisely because they have not been corrupted by the pursuit of money.
The novel's great argument is not about economic systems — it is about whether the soul can survive prosperity.
And then there's the resurrection question — which is, if you think about it, the engine driving the entire plot.
John Harmon is pulled from the river — or is believed to be — and his supposed death sets everything in motion.
But he doesn't stay dead — he returns under assumed identities, watching his own life being lived without him.
And Eugene Wrayburn is pulled from the river half-dead and remade by love and near-death into something approaching a decent human being.
Even Betty Higden flees toward death like it's a kind of freedom — and the river receives her.
The Thames in this novel is simultaneously a sewer, a graveyard, a font of rebirth, and a running commentary on everything money does to people.
That image of the river as a kind of moral mirror for everything money does — I think that brings us perfectly to the other great symbol in this novel, one that's equally strange and equally rich.

The dust heaps — those mountains of Victorian refuse that old Harmon built his fortune on — and the question of what they do to the one man who inherits them: the magnificent, apparently guileless Mr. Boffin.
That's where we're heading next — the dust heaps and Boffin's moral reckoning.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps: Boffin's Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: We've been tracing the dust heaps as an image of wealth accumulated and then redistributed — almost resurrected.
Now I want to turn to the man who inherits all of that dust — and what Dickens does to him morally.
Noddy Boffin is one of the great comic creations in English fiction — and I say that without any qualification.
He arrives on the page like a benevolent gnome — dusty, round, warm, genuinely delighted by almost everything.
And yet Dickens puts him through something quite extraordinary — a staged deterioration that is either profound satire or one of the boldest structural gambits in the Victorian novel.
When Boffin begins his apparent transformation into a miser, obsessively collecting biographies of misers, there is a moment where Dickens gives him this magnificent line.
"I'll read you the lives of the misers, and you shall hear how they lived and how they died, and then judge for yourself whether a man is to be envied or pitied for having money."
It reads at first as ironic self-examination — and then, as the deception unfolds, it reads as something more deliberate and more tender.
What strikes me about Boffin's arc is that it is, at its core, a test — not of society, but of individual character.
Old Harmon's will doesn't simply transfer wealth — it sets a series of trials in motion.
Boffin chooses to enact the role of the corrupted man, sacrificing his own reputation, in order to protect and educate young John Rokesmith and Bella Wilfer.
That is an act of profound moral imagination — of the kind Johnson might have called, without embarrassment, virtue.
Dickens is asking: can goodness survive wealth intact?
And his answer, through Boffin, is a carefully qualified yes — but only through a kind of self-abnegation that most men could not manage.
I want to take Edmund's point seriously — and then push back, just a little.
Yes, Boffin's transformation is ultimately revealed as performance — a calculated ruse to cure Bella of her mercenary values.
But what Dickens is also doing, whether he fully intended it or not, is showing us exactly how wealth operates on perception.
Every single person around Boffin — Wegg, Venus, even Bella herself — sees the money first and the man second.
Silas Wegg's entire scheme of extortion is premised on the assumption that a man with dust-heap money must have obtained it dishonestly.
That is not a moral argument — that is a structural one.
In a world organised around inheritance and the accumulation of waste, suspicion of wealth is simply — rational.
And Wegg is the proof of that, isn't he — because he is both the most cynical and the most comic figure in the whole enterprise.
His wooden leg, his ballad-singing, his literary pretensions — Dickens builds this grotesque with such loving precision.
And yet when Wegg attempts to blackmail Boffin, the novel does something genuinely funny and genuinely devastating at the same time.
Boffin simply — turns the tables.
The moment Wegg is literally tossed out — launched by Mr Venus and the other characters — is pure Dickensian farce operating at the height of its powers.
The physical comedy is the moral verdict.
I'd like to return to something Daniel raised — the question of how others see Boffin once money enters the picture.
There is a passage early in the novel where Dickens describes Boffin as a man who has come suddenly into a great fortune and who wears it, as it were, awkwardly — as if the clothes don't quite fit.
That image of ill-fitting wealth is central to Dickens's moral architecture here.
The truly corrupted characters — Lightwood drifting in his idleness, Podsnap armoured in his complacency — wear their prosperity as if it were a second skin.
Boffin's awkwardness is, in the end, his salvation.
That contrast with Podsnap is exactly the right one to draw.
Podsnappery — and Dickens gives us that magnificent coinage — is wealth that has become ideology.
It is wealth that has forgotten its origins and now mistakes itself for virtue, for Englishness, for the natural order.
Boffin never forgets where his money came from — and crucially, neither does Dickens.
The dust heaps are always there — physically, symbolically — as the source that cannot be aestheticised away.
That is what makes Boffin's moral reckoning so much more interesting than, say, a straightforward inheritance plot.
The wealth is soiled from the start — and yet from that soil something genuinely good is made possible.
What I find most extraordinary — as someone who has actually read this novel aloud, for many hours — is the moment the deception is revealed.
When Mrs Boffin breaks down and confesses the scheme to Bella, the emotional release is enormous — and it catches the reader completely off guard.
Because Dickens has been so committed to the performance of Boffin's greed that even attentive readers have genuinely wondered whether the good man is truly gone.
That is the craft of it — the novelist playing the same game as his character.
Boffin performs miserliness; Dickens performs the dark novel he is not, in fact, writing.
So the dust heap turns out to be not merely a source of corruption but — in Boffin's hands — almost an instrument of moral education.
And the chief pupil in that education is, of course, Bella Wilfer — who receives the full force of Boffin's performance, and is entirely changed by it.
Her story — of a young woman seduced by the idea of wealth, and then slowly, painfully, redeemed — is where we'll turn next.

segments.title: Bella's Golden Cage: Greed and Redemption

utterances.text: We've been talking about Boffin's extraordinary moral performance — the way he weaponises the appearance of greed to test those around him.
And that brings us, naturally, to the character who is most profoundly tested by the spectacle of wealth in this novel: Bella Wilfer.
Bella is one of those characters Dickens absolutely adores — and absolutely refuses to let off the hook.
She arrives in the novel as a young woman who has been left, by a dead man's will, as a kind of human bequest — a legacy to a stranger she's never met.
And her response to this absurd situation is not noble resignation — it's fury, and vanity, and a perfectly frank confession of mercenary desire.
She tells her father — dear old Rumty Wilfer — that she wants to be rich, and that she is determined to marry for money.
"I love money, and want money — want it dreadfully. I hate to be poor, and we are degradingly poor."
The nerve of it! And the honesty — Dickens gives her that honesty, which is what makes her redeemable.
What strikes me as remarkable is how seriously Dickens takes Bella's moral education — it is, in the old sense, a formation of character.
One thinks of the great tradition of the novel of self-knowledge: the character who must be stripped of illusions before they can see clearly.
Bella's flaw is not greed in the abstract — it is what one might call the confusion of value: she has mistaken the price of things for their worth.
And Boffin's household is precisely the environment in which that confusion is made visible — and ultimately, corrected.
What I find genuinely moving is the scene in which she turns upon the apparently corrupted Boffin and defends John Rokesmith.
She has no material reason to take his side — indeed, every financial interest points the other way.
And yet she does. That is the moment Dickens has been building toward — the moment character asserts itself against interest.
I want to sit with the discomfort of Bella's position for a moment longer, because I think Edmund is moving toward the resolution rather too quickly.
When Bella says she wants to be rich, she is not merely expressing a personal failing — she is articulating something the novel knows is structurally produced.
She grew up in Holloway, in that wonderfully named house the Wilfer family calls the Boffin-ish establishment — cramped, respectable, and bitterly insufficient.
Her desire for money is not a moral aberration — it is the perfectly rational response of a clever woman to a society in which women's security depends entirely on the wealth of the men they marry.
Dickens half-knows this, and then pulls back from it — by making her redemption a matter of the heart rather than a transformation of the conditions that produced her desire.
The novel wants her to choose love over money — and she does — but the comfort Dickens provides her is that Harmon turns out to be wealthy after all.
Daniel, you're quite right, and I think Dickens knew it too — there's something slightly sheepish about that ending, isn't there.
But I want to defend the journey, even if the destination is a little too tidy.
There is a scene — the picnic by the water, Bella and her father — which is simply one of the loveliest things Dickens ever wrote.
Old Rumty Wilfer, in his seedy clerk's coat, pretending to be a grand gentleman for his daughter's sake — there's a tenderness there that catches you entirely off guard.
And Bella, in that moment, is not thinking about money at all.
She's thinking about her father's goodness — and that is the seed of everything that follows.
I take Daniel's point about structural conditions — I am not entirely unsympathetic to it.
But I think the novel's moral interest lies precisely in the tension between what society makes of us and what we make of ourselves.
Bella is not the only young woman in her circumstances — and yet she is the one who changes.
There is a moment when she reflects, with great clarity, that she has been "the minx and the hussy" of her own making.
"I have been a wicked creature," she tells Rokesmith, and the simplicity of that confession is precisely what Dickens means by moral growth.
That is not sentiment — that is a genuine reckoning. Character tested and, at last, clarified.
And I'll grant that reckoning is real — Dickens earns it emotionally, even if he flinches from its full implications.
What interests me is the figure of Pa — R. Wilfer — because he is the novel's image of what it means to be good without being rich.
He is threadbare, subordinated, perpetually condescended to by Mrs. Wilfer — and yet he radiates a quiet dignity that no amount of money could manufacture.
Bella's real education is not learning to love Harmon — it is learning to see her father clearly.
The novel keeps returning to that relationship — the picnic, the walks, the conversations — as the counterweight to everything mercenary in the plot.
In that sense, Dickens is more subversive than he appears — he places the moral centre of the novel not in wealth, not in romance, but in a clerk who earns next to nothing.
That's beautifully put — and it connects to something I find endlessly delightful about Mrs. Wilfer.
She is a comic creation of pure genius — this woman who carries about her the permanent air of theatrical tragedy, as though life has done her a catastrophic wrong.
And she has — she's married to Rumty Wilfer, and she will never let him forget it.
But the comedy is not cruel — it's the comedy of a household that is genuinely alive, genuinely particular.
And Bella escaping from it — and then choosing to return to its values, if not its address — is the shape of her whole arc.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is that Bella's story is in some ways the emotional spine of the whole novel — a character who earns her transformation.
And yet her transformation is entangled with a man who has spent the entire novel in disguise — John Rokesmith, otherwise known as John Harmon.
Which brings us to a question we've been circling: what does it mean to hide who you are in a novel so obsessed with the surfaces of wealth and class?
That's where we're headed next — Harmon's masquerade, and what it reveals about identity in Our Mutual Friend.
We've been tracking Bella's slow liberation from the worship of money — but of course, the novel places her inside a household built entirely on concealment.
Which brings us to the man at the centre of that concealment: John Harmon, who spends most of this novel pretending to be someone else entirely.
What strikes me first, as a performer, is just how theatrical the whole Harmon construction is.
He is, in the most literal sense, playing a part — and Dickens knows it, because he gives Harmon a chapter in which he rehearses his own identity like an actor running lines.
That remarkable chapter in the second book — 'A Solo and a Duett' — where Harmon reasons through who he is and who he is pretending to be.
He tells himself: 'I came back, shrunk from my inheritance, and hid myself, and was going to fly from the place where I had hidden, when I found I could not do it.'
The syntax itself mimics the tangle — 'came back, shrunk, hid, was going to fly, found I could not.'
Each verb is a step further into the labyrinth of his own making.
What interests me rather more than the theatrical scaffolding is the moral question underneath it.
Harmon's disguise is not mere trickery — it is a test he sets himself, to discover whether love can exist independent of fortune.
One thinks of the old romance tradition: the prince who hides his rank to find a true-hearted beloved.
What Dickens adds — and this is his genius — is the psychological cost.
Harmon must watch the woman he loves being courted by the very phantom he has invented.
And he must watch the Boffins — good, generous souls — knowingly play out a pretence that would horrify them if they were not themselves part of it.
I think we have to press on what the disguise is actually disguising, though.
John Harmon assumes the name John Rokesmith — a name that means nothing, a man with no property, no history.
And in that condition, he is hired as a secretary — a paid employee in the household that should by rights be his.
Dickens is showing us, with great precision, what a man looks like when he is stripped of inherited wealth.
He becomes legible to society only as a unit of labour.
The romance reading is there, I grant Edmund that — but the social reading cuts right through it.
Daniel's point about labour is sharp — but I keep coming back to the sheer discomfort Dickens builds into the performance of being nobody.
There is a moment when Mrs. Wilfer — magnificent, catastrophically self-important Mrs. Wilfer — treats Rokesmith with that particular brand of condescension reserved for the dependent class.
And Harmon must simply absorb it.
As Dickens puts it, Rokesmith had 'a certain air upon him of knowing that he was a disreputable fellow in the transaction.'
The disguise doesn't just hide his wealth — it makes him complicit in his own humiliation.
That is a comic observation of the darkest kind.
I think Oliver has touched on something rather important — the question of what the masquerade costs Harmon's dignity.
There is a scene one keeps returning to: Harmon's proposal to Bella as Rokesmith — rejected, and rejected with some cruelty.
She tells him he has shown 'an assumption of a right that I altogether repudiate' — words of considerable heat for a woman who is herself dependent on charity.
What Dickens understands is that pride is not the exclusive property of the wealthy.
Bella's pride in that moment is real and recognisable — and so is Harmon's particular wound at being refused by the woman he loves while wearing a false face.
What I find fascinating is that the revelation scene — when Harmon finally discloses himself to the Boffins — is almost anti-climactic.
We might expect a grand theatrical unmasking, but Dickens withholds it from the reader almost entirely.
The reader learns Rokesmith is Harmon through implication, through accumulation — not through a single thunderclap of disclosure.
And that technique has a political logic: identity in this novel is not a stable kernel waiting to be revealed.
It is constructed, performed, and ratified by social recognition — or denied it.
Harmon is only Harmon again when the world agrees to call him that.
Daniel's right that it's cumulative — and I think that's also true of Boffin's performance within the performance.
Because Noddy Boffin, who we are meant to believe has been corrupted by wealth, is himself playing a part.
The novel gives us a box within a box: Harmon concealed inside Rokesmith, and Boffin performing miserliness to test Bella from within the very household Harmon secretly owns.
At the great unravelling, Boffin tells Bella — and the phrase is extraordinary in its plainness — 'I'll give up everything I possess before I'll be beaten by a puppet.'
The puppets are everywhere in this novel — and the puppet-masters, it turns out, are doing it for love.
The layering of deceptions does risk something, one must say.
When the reader learns that Boffin was never truly corrupted — that the miserliness was a stratagem — there is a satisfaction, yes.
But one does wonder whether Dickens has spent rather a lot of the novel's emotional credit on a contrivance.
The scenes of Boffin humiliating Rokesmith are genuinely disturbing — and the retroactive reassurance that it was all arranged feels, to some readers, like a slight of hand.
Edmund's discomfort there is interesting — because I think Dickens wanted readers to feel disturbed and then only partially reassured.
The discomfort is the point: we believed Boffin had been corrupted because the novel has shown us, chapter after chapter, that money does corrupt.
Veneering, Podsnap, the Lammles — these are not recovered.
Boffin's restoration does not cancel the indictment — it throws it into higher relief by contrast.
So the masquerade, by the end, has done its work on all of them — including us as readers, who were fooled right alongside Bella.

And that sense of the novel as a kind of elaborate performance brings us, rather naturally, to its great comic performers — the grotesques and mountebanks who keep the whole machinery spinning with such magnificent vulgarity.

segments.title: Humour and Sleaze: Dickens's Comic Grotesques

utterances.text: We've been deep in the shadows of Harmon's disguise — the novel's serious machinery of identity and deception.
But Our Mutual Friend is also one of the funniest novels in the English language — and some of its funniest figures are also its most disquieting.
Let's talk about the comic grotesques — Silas Wegg, Mr. Venus, the Veneerings — and what Dickens is really doing when he makes us laugh.
The first thing to say is that Silas Wegg is one of the great comic creations in all of Dickens — and that is saying something considerable.
He is a ballad-seller with a wooden leg who cannot actually read very well — and yet sets himself up as a literary man of consequence.
The joke runs through everything he does: the magnificent pretension, the sham learning, the rolling fraudulent delivery of Gibbon's Roman history.
Dickens gives him one of the best lines in the book when Wegg announces to Boffin, with total sincerity, that he is a literary man with a wooden leg.
"A literary man — with a wooden leg — and all Print is open to him."
That rhythm — that triple beat with the pause for the wooden leg — is pure performance writing.
Dickens is writing for the voice, for the timing — he knows exactly where the laugh lands.
But Wegg is funny and sinister simultaneously — and that combination is doing serious work in the novel.
Wegg is a man of absolutely no substance who attaches himself to wealth like a parasite.
When he discovers what he thinks is a will that could dispossess Boffin, his greed becomes entirely undisguised.
And yet we keep laughing — because Dickens makes Wegg's villainy so extravagantly incompetent.
I think the comedy is a kind of ideological anaesthetic — it softens what is actually a portrait of desperate, grasping poverty turned predatory.
Wegg has nothing — a stall, a leg in a jar, ballads nobody wants — and the system has produced exactly this: a man who survives by attaching himself to the rich.
I think Daniel reaches, as he tends to, for the structural explanation when the moral one is perfectly adequate.
Wegg is not a victim of capitalism — Wegg is a scoundrel, and what makes him funny is precisely his vanity.
The wooden leg in the jar of Mr. Venus — a man who literally deals in human bones and articulated skeletons — is a marvellous comic device.
Mr. Venus is melancholy, sentimental, genuinely skilled at his ghoulish trade, and yet entirely unable to win the affection of Pleasant Riderhood.
His lament that she objects to his profession — that she cannot abide the idea of being, as it were, "weighed in the balance and found wanting" among the bones — is quintessentially Dickensian.
Dickens lets Venus articulate his own absurdity with complete sincerity — and that is the comic genius at work.
The humour is never cruel to Venus — it is tender, almost affectionate — which distinguishes Dickens from the satirist who merely despises.
Edmund is absolutely right about Venus — and that tenderness is the key.
When Venus describes his shop — the wires, the jars, the various articulated specimens — he does it with a kind of proprietorial pride that is completely winning.
And then there is the partnership with Wegg — two men conspiring among human remains, plotting to blackmail a millionaire — played entirely for comedy.
The scene where they sit by the fire reading what they believe to be a secret will, Wegg performing Gibbon with growing self-importance, is among the funniest in the book.
Dickens understood that the most effective comic setting is one of complete incongruity — and what is more incongruous than scheming villainy conducted in a shop full of bones?
And then there are the Veneerings — who are grotesque in a very different register entirely.
Wegg and Venus are funny because they are outlandish — their world is bizarre, peripheral, operating in the margins.
The Veneerings are funny because they are entirely respectable — and that respectability is shown to be as hollow as their new furniture.
Everything about them is new — their house, their friends, their silver, their baby — and Dickens names them with that extraordinary precision.
"Mr. and Mrs. Veneering were bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London."
That triple repetition of "bran-new" is devastating — it tells you everything about these people before a single word of dialogue.
They represent the new money of the 1860s — finance capital, without origin, without substance, purchasing social position wholesale.
On the Veneerings I find myself in rare agreement with Daniel — though I would frame it differently.
The Veneerings represent a failure of character — specifically, the substitution of display for substance.
And the dinner table scenes — with Twemlow always present, always bewildered, always the one genuinely well-bred man in the room — are brilliant social satire.
Twemlow is the moral register of those scenes — the man with real manners who cannot quite understand why everyone else is so busy pretending to have them.
And Dickens gives him, at the very end of the novel, his moment of dignified defiance — which strikes me as one of the most satisfying conclusions in Dickens.
A man of good breeding silences a room full of self-important vulgarians — by simply saying what is true.
What I love about the Veneering scenes specifically is the Analytical Chemist — their butler, who disapproves of everything.
Dickens gives us a servant who communicates nothing but silent, total contempt — and it is somehow the funniest running joke in the book.
The butler appears, offers wine, and manages with every gesture to suggest that the whole gathering is beneath his professional dignity.
It is the kind of joke that only works in prose — the sustained, accumulated irony of a functionary who functions only as a silent moral verdict.
And what unites all of these figures — Wegg, Venus, the Veneerings, the Analytical Chemist — is that the comedy is never mere decoration.
In Dickens, the joke is always doing double duty — it is also the argument.
I want to put one more figure on the table before we leave the grotesques — Podsnap.
Mr. Podsnap is not exactly funny in the same way — he is more frightening than amusing, I think.
Podsnappery — Dickens actually coins the word — describes a whole posture toward reality: the refusal to know what is inconvenient to know.
The great Podsnap gesture — the magnificent sweep of the arm that puts unpleasant things behind him — is a political act dressed up as a social manner.
When Dickens writes that Podsnap has "settled that whatever he put behind him he put out of existence," he is describing something genuinely dangerous.
"Whatever he put behind him he put out of existence."
That is not a comic eccentricity — that is the ideology of a ruling class in a single sentence.
Podsnap is, I grant, a harder figure to feel warmly toward — and I think Dickens intends him to be.
But what distinguishes him from the other grotesques is that he is not merely ridiculous — he has power, and he uses it to enforce conformity.
His treatment of Georgiana — that poor, crushed daughter — is the dark underside of all his bluster.
He is funny until you look at what he has done to the people immediately around him — and then he is something considerably less amusing.
That is the characteristic Dickensian move — the comic surface that cracks to reveal genuine suffering underneath.
Comedy and suffering — always entangled in Dickens, and never quite separable from the larger design of the novel.
Which is perhaps the ideal note on which to turn to the architecture of the whole: the plot, the themes, and the transformations that carry Our Mutual Friend from its murky opening to its resolution.

segments.title: The Book's Backbone: Plot, Theme, and Transformation Across the Arc

utterances.text: We've been delighting in Dickens's grotesques and comedians — but behind all that magnificent noise, there is a spine.
This novel has an architecture — and I want to spend some time with it now, because the plot of Our Mutual Friend is doing something quite remarkable.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is the sheer audacity of the central device.
John Harmon — the heir to the dust mounds — fakes his own death before the novel has barely drawn breath.
And then he spends the entire novel disguised as Rokesmith, watching the woman he's supposed to marry, watching her become someone he genuinely falls in love with.
It's a romantic comedy device that Dickens transforms into a meditation on identity.
Who are we when we strip the name and the fortune away?
Harmon's self-description in that extraordinary chapter of self-examination — 'I, JOHN HARMON, DISGRACED AND DEGRADED' — is one of the strangest, most modern passages Dickens ever wrote.
I would say the Harmon plot is only half the spine, Oliver.
The novel's true backbone is the story of Eugene Wrayburn — and what happens to a man of complete moral idleness when he is forced by circumstance to become something more than he intended.
Wrayburn is, at the novel's opening, genuinely dangerous.
His pursuit of Lizzie Hexam is not admirable — it is the casual predation of the privileged on the vulnerable.
And yet Dickens does something profoundly interesting with him — he earns his redemption through suffering.
Bradley Headstone's assault nearly kills him, and in that near-death, something is genuinely remade.
The novel insists that transformation is possible — but that it costs something real.
Edmund, I want to take that word 'transformation' and put it under some pressure.
Because who gets to be transformed in this novel, and who doesn't?
Harmon gets to reclaim his fortune and his identity.
Wrayburn gets the girl and a second chance at being a gentleman.
Bella Wilfer transforms from a woman who prizes money above all into one who discovers she prizes love — and is rewarded with both.
But Bradley Headstone — the man who worked hardest of all, who clawed himself up through sheer grinding effort — he is destroyed.
And Charlie Hexam, who also struggled up, becomes a calculating little trimmer who abandons his own sister.
The pattern is not random — the system rewards those who already had some cushion and crushes those who had none.
Daniel, you are absolutely right about Headstone — and I think Dickens knew it was the most disturbing portrait in the book.
Here is a man who has memorised everything — turned himself into a kind of human encyclopedia — and it has given him nothing but a capacity for violence.
There's that extraordinary passage where Dickens describes him as having 'acquired mechanically a great store of teacher's knowledge' — the word 'mechanically' doing all the work.
It's not education — it's accumulation without formation.
And then this repressed, over-controlled man falls catastrophically in love with Lizzie Hexam, who barely notices him.
It's almost unbearable to read — he goes from schoolmaster to stalker to murderer with a horrible, logical inevitability.
And the dust mounds themselves — let's not lose sight of them, because they anchor everything.
Old Harmon's fortune built from the accumulated rubbish of London — what does that say about wealth in this novel?
The dust mounds are Dickens's most brilliant single invention in this novel, I think.
They are literal — heaps of ash and cinders and refuse from which a fortune has been sifted — and they are also unmistakably figurative.
Every great fortune in Dickens, when you scrape at it, has this quality — it is built on what others have discarded or what has been taken from those with no voice.
But I resist the purely allegorical reading.
The dust mounds work because they are also simply strange and vivid — mounds of rubbish presiding over a novel about status, inheritance, and the question of what we owe the dead.
The river and the dust — death and accumulation — they press against each other throughout the entire book.
I want to push on the question of inheritance, because the novel's plot is fundamentally driven by what a dead man wanted.
Old Harmon's will is an act of control from beyond the grave — forcing his son to marry a woman he's never met in order to receive the money.
And when young Harmon resists that — when he stages his own death rather than comply — the novel seems to be cheering for him.
But then — and this is where Dickens is genuinely subversive — he still gets the girl and the money in the end.
The system bends just enough to accommodate one fortunate rebel, while everyone without his advantages is ground down.
The Veneerings throw their dinner parties, the Podsnaps pronounce on the destiny of England, and the Thames keeps rolling bodies through London.
Dickens sees the whole picture — even when his plot rewards only a few figures within it.
What I find endlessly fascinating is what the novel does with Bella Wilfer's arc — because that's the emotional centre for most readers.
She begins the novel furious at being left as a legacy — a human bequest — by a man she never knew.
She tells her father she wants to be rich — and she means it, she is marvellously unashamed about it.
Dickens doesn't punish her for that frankness — he rather admires it.
Her scenes with Pa — old Rumty Wilfer — are among the most genuinely tender in the book.
And her transformation is convincing precisely because it is gradual — she doesn't simply decide to be good; she watches Rokesmith and slowly comes to understand what goodness looks like in practice.
That is exactly right, Oliver — and it speaks to what I take to be the novel's deepest theme.
Which is not, in the end, about class or capital — it is about the education of the self.
Character after character in this novel is tested by the question: what do you love — truly love — and what will you sacrifice for it?
Bella chooses Rokesmith over wealth, and the novel rewards her.
Wrayburn, at the very last, chooses to do right by Lizzie, and the novel lets him live.
Headstone chooses obsession over dignity, and the novel sweeps him into the river along with Rogue Riderhood.
There is a moral geometry operating here that I find deeply satisfying — it is austere, but it is not arbitrary.
Edmund's moral geometry is real — I won't deny it — but I think the novel is most alive at the edges of that geometry.
Jenny Wren — the dolls' dressmaker, this small, suffering, fiercely intelligent girl — doesn't fit neatly into any arc of transformation.
She endures. She is sharp and strange and visionary — she talks about the children on the rooftop, the dead coming back good — and the novel doesn't know quite what to do with her.
Lizzie Hexam similarly — the novel's moral beauty is supposed to reside in her, yet she has less interiority than almost any other major character.
The women from the river — they are the novel's conscience, but the novel can't quite bring itself to give them a plot that matches their weight.
That is a structural tension that runs all the way through Our Mutual Friend — and I think it's worth sitting with rather than smoothing over.
That tension — between what the novel rewards and what the novel knows — feels like exactly the right place to arrive at.
Because what we haven't yet asked is the largest question of all: what does this novel ultimately demand of us as readers?
That's what we're going to take up in our final conversation.

segments.title: Closing: What Our Mutual Friend Demands of Us

utterances.text: We've traced the great arc of this novel — the transformations, the resurrections, the relentless turning of the wheel.
But I want to end by asking something that feels almost impertinent: what does Our Mutual Friend actually demand of its reader?
It demands patience, first of all — and I say that as someone who adores every page.
This is a long book, and Dickens makes you earn the satisfactions.
But the other thing it demands is a willingness to hold comedy and grief in the same hand simultaneously.
Think of Silas Wegg — that magnificent, preposterous villain, stumping about on his wooden leg, reciting poetry with magisterial inaccuracy.
He is hilarious, and he is also a study in the corrosive power of resentment — a man who has built his entire identity on grievance.
Dickens asks you to laugh and to recognise something genuinely bleak — at exactly the same moment.
What the novel demands of us, I would argue, is moral seriousness — the willingness to sit with characters who fail and to ask why.
Eugene Wrayburn is the clearest case.
He begins the novel in a condition that the Victorians would have recognised as acedia — that particular paralysis of will that afflicts the clever and purposeless.
Dickens does not excuse him, but he does redeem him — and the instrument of redemption is suffering, very nearly unto death.
That is not a comfortable moral structure for a modern reader.
It asks us to believe that character can change — not through therapy or self-expression — but through genuine crisis and the love of a good woman.
One may find that old-fashioned.
I find it rather bracing.
I think the novel demands something more uncomfortable than moral seriousness — it demands that we see the system.
Dickens keeps bringing us back to the dust heaps — that great fortune built on the accumulated refuse of London.
And he is asking: where does wealth come from?
Not from virtue, not from intelligence — from the dross that the city cannot use and somebody thought to collect.
The Lammles — that extraordinary pair — marry each other for money neither of them possesses, and spend the novel swindling others to survive their own swindle.
That is not satire exactly — that is a structural description of how a speculative economy actually functions.
The novel demands we feel the weight of that — not just laugh at the Veneerings and move on.
Let me push all three of you on a specific question about the novel's final emotional register.
Does Our Mutual Friend end with hope — or with something more guarded than that?
Guarded is exactly the word, I think — and that is what makes it feel so truthful compared to the earlier novels.
Bella and John Harmon get their happiness — and it is genuinely warm, genuinely earned.
But Jenny Wren is still Jenny Wren — still bearing her drunken father, still fashioning her little dolls in a world that has no proper place for her.
And Riah goes back to his service — dignified, honourable, and still subject to Fledgeby's cruelty for most of the book.
Dickens gives with one hand and withholds with the other — and I think he does so deliberately.
The happily-ever-afters are real, but they are not universal — and Dickens knows you've noticed.
I would put it slightly differently.
The novel ends with a kind of provisional grace — not triumphant, but sufficient.
Consider the Postscript — the one Dickens appended after finishing — in which he mentions the Staplehurst railway accident almost without drama.
He was in that crash.
He crawled back into wreckage to retrieve manuscript pages of this very novel — and he mentions this with barely a shrug.
That is the tone of the whole novel's ending, I think — a man who has looked at the worst and decided to complete the work anyway.
Not cheerful.
Resolved.
Edmund's point about the Postscript is important, but I want to press on what the novel does with its most radical figure.
Betty Higden.
This old woman walks herself to death across the countryside rather than enter the workhouse — rather than submit to the Poor Law.
Dickens is not being sentimental about her death — he is being furious.
He is saying: a system that makes death preferable to institutional charity is not a welfare system — it is a punishment system.
Betty Higden does not appear in the happy endings, because she is not a problem the happy endings can solve.
That is what the novel demands of us: to remember her even as we celebrate the Harmons.
Daniel has put his finger on something extraordinary there — and it connects to the river.
The Thames runs through this novel as a constant fact — not a symbol exactly, but a presence.
It gives and it takes.
Gaffer Hexam makes his living from the dead it offers up.
John Harmon is supposedly drowned in it and reborn from it.
Rogue Riderhood is dragged back from its depths — and comes back worse than before, which is Dickens at his most merciless.
The river is indifferent — and in a novel so full of people calculating and scheming, that indifference feels almost like justice.
The river also provides the novel's most purely beautiful writing, I would contend.
There is the passage where Dickens describes the boat moving through London at night — the lights on the water, the darkness between them.
He writes of the river as though it were the unconscious life of the city — everything the daylight refuses to acknowledge, moving darkly beneath.
That is not social critique — or not only that.
That is a writer at the full stretch of his imaginative power — which is where I would always rather dwell.
I won't fight Edmund on the prose — he's right about the night passages.
But what I keep returning to, in the end, is Lizzie Hexam.
She is the most quietly radical figure in the novel — a working-class woman who refuses every category the world assigns her.
She will not be merely her father's daughter — she educates herself, she protects her brother, she saves Eugene's life.
And yet her marriage to Eugene — the novel's great romantic resolution — is also the moment the social hierarchy reasserts itself.
She rises by attaching herself to a man of class — and the novel seems unaware of the tension.
That is what makes it a great Victorian novel rather than a revolutionary one.
Though I would say — and this might be my performer's instinct speaking — that Dickens put something in Eugene's degradation that he couldn't quite name.
The scene on his sickbed — when he is barely conscious and struggling to find the word to describe Lizzie — is one of the strangest, most tender scenes in all of Dickens.
He calls her — with immense effort — his wife.
And the social world does not quite know what to do with that — nor does the novel, entirely.
But I think that uncertainty is the most honest thing in the book.
So perhaps what the novel finally demands is this: that we hold its contradictions without resolving them.
The dust heaps and the drawing rooms.
Betty Higden walking to her death and Bella Wilfer dancing with her baby.
Silas Wegg tumbling into the cart and Eugene Wrayburn, broken and remade, saying the word that reorders his world.
That is the novel's demand — and its gift.
My profound thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Daniel Rosen — three readers who have made this book live again in quite different ways, and all the better for it.
We have roamed the dust heaps and the river, the Veneering table and the dolls' dressmaker's garret — and I hope you have felt, as I have, the full strange weight of this extraordinary novel.
Our Mutual Friend is not a comfortable book.
It is a necessary one.
Thank you for listening.

c4:p48.text:
‘You are a chit and a little idiot,’ returned Bella, ‘or you wouldn’t make
      such a dolly speech. What did you expect me to do? Wait till you are a
      woman, and don’t talk about what you don’t understand. You only show your
      ignorance!’ Then, whimpering again, and at intervals biting the curls, and
      stopping to look how much was bitten off, ‘It’s a shame! There never was
      such a hard case! I shouldn’t care so much if it wasn’t so ridiculous. It
      was ridiculous enough to have a stranger coming over to marry me, whether
      he liked it or not. It was ridiculous enough to know what an embarrassing
      meeting it would be, and how we never could pretend to have an inclination
      of our own, either of us. It was ridiculous enough to know I shouldn’t
      like him—how  could  I like him, left to him in a will, like a dozen
      of spoons, with everything cut and dried beforehand, like orange chips.
      Talk of orange flowers indeed! I declare again it’s a shame! Those
      ridiculous points would have been smoothed away by the money, for I love
      money, and want money—want it dreadfully. I hate to be poor, and we
      are degradingly poor, offensively poor, miserably poor, beastly poor. But
      here I am, left with all the ridiculous parts of the situation remaining,
      and, added to them all, this ridiculous dress! And if the truth was known,
      when the Harmon murder was all over the town, and people were speculating
      on its being suicide, I dare say those impudent wretches at the clubs and
      places made jokes about the miserable creature’s having preferred a watery
      grave to me. It’s likely enough they took such liberties; I shouldn’t
      wonder! I declare it’s a very hard case indeed, and I am a most
      unfortunate girl. The idea of being a kind of a widow, and never having
      been married! And the idea of being as poor as ever after all, and going
      into black, besides, for a man I never saw, and should have hated—as
      far as  he  was concerned—if I had seen!’
c4:p48.summary: Bella unleashes a torrent of complaint: the arranged marriage to a stranger was absurd, his death was embarrassing, and now she is stuck mourning him in ridiculous black dress while remaining poor. She passionately declares her love of money and her horror at their degrading poverty, then suggests people mocked her for the Harmon's suicide (presumably), and concludes that being a 'widow' who was never married is the ultimate injustice.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

c24:p88.text:
Mr Wegg then goes on to enlarge upon what throughout has been uppermost in
      his crafty mind:—the qualifications of Mr Venus for such a search.
      He expatiates on Mr Venus’s patient habits and delicate manipulation; on
      his skill in piecing little things together; on his knowledge of various
      tissues and textures; on the likelihood of small indications leading him
      on to the discovery of great concealments. ‘While as to myself,’ says
      Wegg, ‘I am not good at it. Whether I gave myself up to prodding, or
      whether I gave myself up to scooping, I couldn’t do it with that delicate
      touch so as not to show that I was disturbing the mounds. Quite different
      with  you , going to work (as  you  would) in the light of a fellow-man,
      holily pledged in a friendly move to his brother man.’ Mr Wegg next
      modestly remarks on the want of adaptation in a wooden leg to ladders and
      such like airy perches, and also hints at an inherent tendency in that
      timber fiction, when called into action for the purposes of a promenade on
      an ashey slope, to stick itself into the yielding foothold, and peg its
      owner to one spot. Then, leaving this part of the subject, he remarks on
      the special phenomenon that before his installation in the Bower, it was
      from Mr Venus that he first heard of the legend of hidden wealth in the
      Mounds: ‘which’, he observes with a vaguely pious air, ‘was surely never
      meant for nothing.’ Lastly, he returns to the cause of the right, gloomily
      foreshadowing the possibility of something being unearthed to criminate Mr
      Boffin (of whom he once more candidly admits it cannot be denied that he
      profits by a murder), and anticipating his denunciation by the friendly
      movers to avenging justice. And this, Mr Wegg expressly points out, not at
      all for the sake of the reward—though it would be a want of
      principle not to take it.
c24:p88.summary: Wegg elaborates on Venus's qualifications for the search—his patience, delicate touch, skill at reconstruction—while admitting his own limitations and hinting at Boffin's culpability.

c2:p24.text:
The great looking-glass above the sideboard, reflects the table and the
      company. Reflects the new Veneering crest, in gold and eke in silver,
      frosted and also thawed, a camel of all work. The Heralds’ College found
      out a Crusading ancestor for Veneering who bore a camel on his shield (or
      might have done it if he had thought of it), and a caravan of camels take
      charge of the fruits and flowers and candles, and kneel down to be loaded
      with the salt. Reflects Veneering; forty, wavy-haired, dark, tending to
      corpulence, sly, mysterious, filmy—a kind of sufficiently
      well-looking veiled-prophet, not prophesying. Reflects Mrs Veneering;
      fair, aquiline-nosed and fingered, not so much light hair as she might
      have, gorgeous in raiment and jewels, enthusiastic, propitiatory,
      conscious that a corner of her husband’s veil is over herself. Reflects
      Podsnap; prosperously feeding, two little light-coloured wiry wings, one
      on either side of his else bald head, looking as like his hairbrushes as
      his hair, dissolving view of red beads on his forehead, large allowance of
      crumpled shirt-collar up behind. Reflects Mrs Podsnap; fine woman for
      Professor Owen, quantity of bone, neck and nostrils like a rocking-horse,
      hard features, majestic head-dress in which Podsnap has hung golden
      offerings. Reflects Twemlow; grey, dry, polite, susceptible to east wind,
      First-Gentleman-in-Europe collar and cravat, cheeks drawn in as if he had
      made a great effort to retire into himself some years ago, and had got so
      far and had never got any farther. Reflects mature young lady; raven
      locks, and complexion that lights up well when well powdered—as it
      is—carrying on considerably in the captivation of mature young
      gentleman; with too much nose in his face, too much ginger in his
      whiskers, too much torso in his waistcoat, too much sparkle in his studs,
      his eyes, his buttons, his talk, and his teeth. Reflects charming old Lady
      Tippins on Veneering’s right; with an immense obtuse drab oblong face,
      like a face in a tablespoon, and a dyed Long Walk up the top of her head,
      as a convenient public approach to the bunch of false hair behind, pleased
      to patronize Mrs Veneering opposite, who is pleased to be patronized.
      Reflects a certain ‘Mortimer’, another of Veneering’s oldest friends; who
      never was in the house before, and appears not to want to come again, who
      sits disconsolate on Mrs Veneering’s left, and who was inveigled by Lady
      Tippins (a friend of his boyhood) to come to these people’s and talk, and
      who won’t talk. Reflects Eugene, friend of Mortimer; buried alive in the
      back of his chair, behind a shoulder—with a powder-epaulette on it—of
      the mature young lady, and gloomily resorting to the champagne chalice
      whenever proffered by the Analytical Chemist. Lastly, the looking-glass
      reflects Boots and Brewer, and two other stuffed Buffers interposed
      between the rest of the company and possible accidents.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

      by M. R. F. that he should have a mechanical genius. And so on. Therefore

‘Hardly so, I think,’ the stubborn Mortimer strikes in. ‘I take the
      question to be, whether such a man as you describe, Lady Tippins, does
      right or wrong in marrying a brave woman (I say nothing of her beauty),

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c67:p58.text:
To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
c67:p58.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.
c67:p58.best_quote: To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design.

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.

In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.

c20:p53.text:
Probably because this reason is in the air, Twemlow, far from being
      singular in his persuasion that he works like a Trojan, is capped by
      Podsnap, who in his turn is capped by Boots and Brewer. At eight o’clock
      when all these hard workers assemble to dine at Veneering’s, it is
      understood that the cabs of Boots and Brewer mustn’t leave the door, but
      that pails of water must be brought from the nearest baiting-place, and
      cast over the horses’ legs on the very spot, lest Boots and Brewer should
      have instant occasion to mount and away. Those fleet messengers require
      the Analytical to see that their hats are deposited where they can be laid
      hold of at an instant’s notice; and they dine (remarkably well though)
      with the air of firemen in charge of an engine, expecting intelligence of
      some tremendous conflagration.

c33:p48.text:
However, the great subject of the happiness of Mr and Mrs Lammle must not
      be allowed to vanish with the other vanishments—with the vanishing
      of the murderer, the vanishing of Julius Handford, the vanishing of Lizzie
      Hexam,—and therefore Veneering must recall the present sheep to the
      pen from which they have strayed. Who so fit to discourse of the happiness
      of Mr and Mrs Lammle, they being the dearest and oldest friends he has in
      the world; or what audience so fit for him to take into his confidence as
      that audience, a noun of multitude or signifying many, who are all the
      oldest and dearest friends he has in the world? So Veneering, without the
      formality of rising, launches into a familiar oration, gradually toning
      into the Parliamentary sing-song, in which he sees at that board his dear
      friend Twemlow who on that day twelvemonth bestowed on his dear friend
      Lammle the fair hand of his dear friend Sophronia, and in which he also
      sees at that board his dear friends Boots and Brewer whose rallying round
      him at a period when his dear friend Lady Tippins likewise rallied round
      him—ay, and in the foremost rank—he can never forget while
      memory holds her seat. But he is free to confess that he misses from that
      board his dear old friend Podsnap, though he is well represented by his
      dear young friend Georgiana. And he further sees at that board (this he
      announces with pomp, as if exulting in the powers of an extraordinary
      telescope) his friend Mr Fledgeby, if he will permit him to call him so.
      For all of these reasons, and many more which he right well knows will
      have occurred to persons of your exceptional acuteness, he is here to
      submit to you that the time has arrived when, with our hearts in our
      glasses, with tears in our eyes, with blessings on our lips, and in a
      general way with a profusion of gammon and spinach in our emotional
      larders, we should one and all drink to our dear friends the Lammles,
      wishing them many years as happy as the last, and many many friends as
      congenially united as themselves. And this he will add; that Anastatia
      Veneering (who is instantly heard to weep) is formed on the same model as
      her old and chosen friend Sophronia Lammle, in respect that she is devoted
      to the man who wooed and won her, and nobly discharges the duties of a
      wife.
c33:p48.summary: Veneering delivers an extended, self-congratulatory oration celebrating the Lammles' marriage and the assembled company's friendship, filled with parliamentary bombast and hypocritical sentiment.
c33:p48.best_quote: a profusion of gammon and spinach in our emotional larders

c67:p61.text:
On Friday the Ninth of June in the present year, Mr and Mrs Boffin (in
      their manuscript dress of receiving Mr and Mrs Lammle at breakfast) were
      on the South Eastern Railway with me, in a terribly destructive accident.
      When I had done what I could to help others, I climbed back into my
      carriage—nearly turned over a viaduct, and caught aslant upon the
      turn—to extricate the worthy couple. They were much soiled, but
      otherwise unhurt. The same happy result attended Miss Bella Wilfer on her
      wedding day, and Mr Riderhood inspecting Bradley Headstone’s red
      neckerchief as he lay asleep. I remember with devout thankfulness that I
      can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I
      was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with
      which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
c67:p61.summary: Dickens recounts his experience in the Staplehurst railway accident of June 9, 1865, expressing gratitude for his miraculous escape and reflecting on mortality in connection with the novel's conclusion.
